For transport covered by the regulation, exceeding prescribed driving times incurs a fine; the amount depends on the infringement.

After four and a half hours of driving, a break of at least 45 minutes is required unless a rest period begins; it can be split into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30. Failure to take the prescribed breaks incurs a penalty.
For services where it is required, the extract concerns the schedule established in advance for driving, other work, breaks and availability. Its absence, incompleteness or alteration is penalized.

A regular daily rest period is at least 11 hours; under certain conditions it can be reduced to at least 9. During rest the driver can freely dispose of their time; failing to take the prescribed rest is penalized.
Exceeding driving times incurs a fine, not automatic revocation of the driving licence; documents may be temporarily withdrawn until the required rest is taken.

Four consecutive hours, considered alone, do not exceed the four-and-a-half-hour limit. After four and a half hours of driving, an uninterrupted break of at least 45 minutes is required before driving resumes, unless a rest period begins. Alternatively, the break may be split during the driving period into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30. For occasional passenger services, two breaks of at least 15 minutes each, totaling at least 45 minutes, are also permitted.
An analogue record sheet must not be used beyond its intended recording period: a 24-hour sheet must be replaced within that period to avoid overlapping records.
Exceeding driving times incurs a fine; it does not automatically lead to revocation of the driver qualification card.
For transport within its scope, the regulation sets driving limits as well as breaks and rest periods.
The regulation includes a weekly limit: driving time must not exceed 56 hours in a week.
The regulation limits maximum driving time; it does not require a minimum number of driving hours.
The rules cover both goods and passenger transport, within their respective scopes.
For goods, the general threshold is a maximum permissible mass over 3.5 tonnes, including any trailer or semi-trailer; exclusions apply.
The rules cover vehicles designed or adapted to carry more than nine people including the driver and intended for that purpose; exclusions apply.

The 2025 quiz marks this FALSE: the general goods-transport threshold is over 3.5 tonnes, including a trailer. Since 1 July 2026, over 2.5 tonnes also covers certain international or cabotage operations, subject to exceptions such as qualifying own-account transport.
The scope includes certain passenger vehicles as well as goods vehicles.
The normal daily driving limit is nine hours; it may rise to ten no more than twice a week.
Daily driving can reach ten hours at most twice a week; the normal limit is nine hours.
Nine hours is a normal daily driving limit, not a consecutive driving period: after four and a half hours a break is required unless a rest period begins.
The normal extension permitted twice a week is to ten hours, not eleven.
Breaks do not authorize twelve hours of daily driving: the normal limit is nine hours, extendable to ten at most twice a week.
Regular daily rest comprises at least eleven hours; it can also be split into at least three hours followed by at least nine.
A reduced daily rest is at least 9 but less than 11 hours. At most three are permitted between two weekly rests; that interval does not necessarily match the calendar week.
The limit of three reduced daily rests is counted between two weekly rest periods, not simply by calendar week.
Daily rest has its own durations: regular rest is at least eleven hours, while reduced rest is at least nine and less than eleven. It need not equal driving time.
During rest the driver can freely dispose of their time; this distinguishes it from work.
The 45 minutes are a driving break, not reduced daily rest, which lasts at least 9 hours and less than 11.
Regular weekly rest consists of at least 45 consecutive hours, unlike reduced rest.
There are two forms: regular rest of at least 45 hours and reduced rest of at least 24 consecutive hours, subject to the applicable conditions.

The quiz marks this FALSE: 30 hours is not enough for a regular weekly rest, which must last at least 45 hours. A 30-hour rest may instead count as a reduced weekly rest if the applicable conditions and compensation requirements are met.
The 24 hours are the minimum, not the maximum: reduced rest lasts less than 45 hours and at least 24 consecutive hours.
The minimum regular weekly rest is 45 consecutive hours, not 90.
Weekly rest is mandatory: payment cannot replace the required rest time.
During availability the driver need not remain at the workstation, but must be ready to resume work; its foreseeable duration is known in advance.
When a vehicle is multi-manned, time spent beside the driver or in a bunk while it is travelling is availability.
Other work includes work activities other than driving, such as cleaning and maintenance; it is recorded separately from driving.
Being free to dispose of time characterizes rest. During availability the driver must be ready to resume work.
Cleaning the vehicle is a work activity and counts as other work, not availability.
Vehicle ownership does not exempt the driver from penalties for their own infringements; the undertaking may also be liable under the applicable rules.
Responsibility does not rest solely with the driver: the undertaking is also liable under applicable provisions and must give instructions compatible with the limits.

To safeguard the safety of people, the vehicle or the load, the limits may be exceeded only as much as necessary to reach a suitable stopping place, without compromising road safety. Article 12 separately provides for an exceptional, conditional exemption to reach the driver's home or the employer's operational centre for weekly rest.
When using the exemption to reach a suitable stopping place, the reason must be recorded by hand on the record sheet or printout, no later than on arrival at the stopping place.

The quiz marks this FALSE: going home does not normally permit exceeding the limits. In exceptional circumstances, without jeopardising road safety, Article 12 permits return to the driver’s residence or employer’s operational centre for weekly rest: up to one extra hour, or two for regular weekly rest after an uninterrupted 30-minute break immediately before the extra driving. The reason must be recorded and the extension compensated by the end of the third following week.

The quiz marks this FALSE: reaching the vehicle owner’s depot does not normally permit exceeding the limits. In exceptional circumstances, without jeopardising road safety, Article 12 permits return to the driver’s residence or employer’s operational centre for weekly rest, not just any owner’s depot: up to one extra hour, or two for regular weekly rest after an uninterrupted 30-minute break immediately before the extra driving. The reason must be recorded and the extension compensated by the end of the third following week.
A break is used exclusively for recuperation: the driver neither drives nor does other work during it.
Rest is an uninterrupted period during which the driver can freely dispose of their time, without remaining available for work.
A stop is not automatically a break: a break must be devoted exclusively to recuperation, without driving or other work.
Availability does not mean agreeing to work overtime: it is a period distinct from breaks and rest when the worker is ready to respond to a call, under the prescribed conditions.
The ordinary weekly driving limit is 56 hours; the limit of 90 hours in two consecutive weeks also applies.

The ordinary weekly driving limit is 56 hours; the maximum over two consecutive weeks is 90 hours. The exceptional return derogation for reaching the driver’s residence or employer’s operational centre can extend the weekly limit under its conditions, but not the 90-hour limit.
Regular weekly rest is at least 45 hours. It must normally begin within six 24-hour periods after the end of the previous weekly rest; reduced rest is also allowed under legal conditions.
Reduced weekly rest lasts at least 24 hours; the reduction must be compensated in one block by the end of the third following week, subject to the other weekly rest conditions.
The order is reversed: split regular daily rest starts with at least 3 consecutive hours, followed by at least 9.
The ordinary rule does not require 48 hours after four driving periods: regular weekly rest is at least 45 hours and normally starts within six 24-hour periods after the previous weekly rest.
The ordinary weekly driving limit is 56 hours, not 48; the 90-hour limit over two consecutive weeks also applies.

The ordinary weekly limit is 56 hours, but the maximum over two consecutive weeks is 90 hours, not 100. The exceptional return derogation for reaching the driver’s residence or employer’s operational centre can extend the weekly limit under its conditions, but not the 90-hour limit.
The device records both the driver’s driving activity and vehicle movement data, including speed.
The different activities are recorded separately; the driver selects or enters periods other than driving as appropriate.
The tachograph records distance traveled and speed: these data let inspectors check vehicle movement alongside the driver’s activity periods.
The tachograph records movement data and driver activity, not conversations.
Recording is not started by pressing a START button on the dashboard: the driver uses a sheet or card and records activities according to the device’s procedures.

The tachograph records data such as distance and speed, not the complete path taken by the vehicle. A smart tachograph also retains specific positions, for example at the start and end of the working day: individual points do not describe the entire route.

Goods transport over 3.5 tonnes generally falls within the obligation, subject to exemptions. Since July 1, 2026, certain international transport or cabotage operations over 2.5 tonnes are also covered.
The exemption applies to regular passenger services whose route is no longer than 50 km. Use for a non-regular service does not automatically qualify for that exemption and may require a tachograph.

Not all goods vehicles are covered: mass, type of transport and exemptions matter. The general threshold is over 3.5 tonnes; since July 1, 2026, certain international transport or cabotage operations are covered above 2.5 tonnes.
Regular passenger services on routes of no more than 50 km are exempt from EU driving-time rules and the related tachograph requirement.
Specialised breakdown vehicles operating within 100 km of their base are exempt from EU driving-time rules and the related tachograph requirement.
Under normal storage conditions, the sheet’s records must remain clearly legible for at least one year.
The 24 hours are the sheet’s minimum recording capacity, not necessarily its exact duration: the capacity may be greater.
The sheet provides space for handwritten details, such as the driver’s name and the vehicle registration number.
The required minimum capacity is 24 hours, not 48; several discs can be linked to increase it.
The switch allows activities such as other work, availability and rest to be recorded separately; driving time is recorded automatically.
Record the time of the vehicle change on the chart so the record can be linked to the vehicles used.
Enter the registration of every vehicle used, including the one taken over after the change.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but does not clearly distinguish distance travelled from the odometer reading. The initial and final readings are entered on the chart; their difference gives the kilometres travelled, which can be written down, but a separate total is not required by the regulation.
The chart follows the driver's activity: it should be kept for checks, not left in the vehicle at the end of the working period.
For a change, enter the time of the vehicle change, not the start time of the shift as the change detail.
The pictured square with a diagonal indicates availability. Select the bed symbol for rest.
The figure shown does not match the crossed hammers: on a tachograph, these indicate other work, such as loading and unloading.
The chart must be type-approved and compatible with the tachograph so its recordings suit the equipment used.
The initial details identify the driver, vehicle and start of chart use; the initial reading later helps establish the distance.
Document the change with the time, registration and odometer readings of both vehicles in the spaces provided on the chart.
Use approved charts suitable for the tachograph model, not just any chart.
The driver's first and last names are required, but driving licence and CQC details are not required entries on the analogue chart.
The driver's name and registration are analogue chart details; tachograph card details are not required to fill it in.
The digital tachograph records data in the unit's memory and on the inserted driver card, according to their respective functions.

The quiz marks this TRUE: some devices can also sound a warning when driving without the appropriate card. The regulation requires a visual warning; sound is additional and is not mandatory on every device.
The data can be printed: the digital tachograph has a printer for the required printouts.
The card covers the period when the driver uses the vehicle: insert it at the start and withdraw it at the end of the working period, except where authorised.
The personal driver card has a white background, distinguishing it from other tachograph cards.
In Italy, the competent Chamber of Commerce issues the driver card after checking eligibility.
The device permits card withdrawal only when the vehicle is stopped, after storing the relevant data on it.
The company card serves the company’s functions and cannot replace the driver’s personal card. If it is lost, request a replacement and make the required records.
The control card is for enforcement officers to check data; it is not a driver’s maintenance tool.
The workshop card is for persons authorised to work on the tachograph, not the driver repairing the vehicle.
Tachograph installation is reserved for fitters or workshops approved by the competent authorities.
The seals protect the integrity of the installation: the driver must not tamper with the tachograph or alter its records.
Calibration adapts the tachograph to the vehicle’s characteristics and is part of installation before entry into service.
The installation plaque records technical installation data, which are also useful for subsequent inspections.
The tachograph must be inspected at least every two years; some events require an earlier inspection.
Equipment alone is not enough: tachograph inspection requires an approved workshop.
Tachograph repair requires an approved fitter or workshop, not just any mechanical workshop.
Calibration is part of installation before entry into service: there is no general four-week period after installation.
Periodic inspection is required at least every two years, or earlier in certain circumstances.
Even a serious tachograph fault must be repaired by an approved fitter or workshop.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but the time limit runs from the failure, not the total length of the trip. An approved repair must be made as soon as circumstances permit; if the vehicle cannot return to the undertaking’s premises within a week of the breakdown or its discovery, it must be repaired en route.
A faulty tachograph must be repaired by an approved fitter or workshop as soon as circumstances permit.
During the breakdown the driver manually records activities no longer correctly recorded or printed, identifying themselves and signing the entries.

There is no general 24-hour deadline: repair must be made as soon as possible and, if the vehicle cannot return to base within one week of the breakdown or discovery of defective operation, during the journey.
A breakdown does not always require the journey to stop immediately: manual records and repair as soon as possible are required under the applicable conditions.
Tachograph repair requires an approved fitter or workshop; the Chamber of Commerce issues cards and does not perform this repair.
The tachograph records vehicle data such as distance and speed, and the driver’s activity periods, including driving and rest.
The device has slots for the driver and co-driver and can record both their activities.
The tachograph printer can produce paper printouts of vehicle memory or card data, including daily activities.
It also records vehicle data, such as distance and speed, as well as driver activities.
A complete record of the last five years is not guaranteed: capacity varies by data type, and the oldest data are replaced when the allocated memory is full.
The tachograph can print daily activities recorded on the driver card or in the vehicle unit memory.
The microprocessor card interacts with the tachograph; the driver card stores changes of activity, among other information.
The driver card also stores data about vehicles used, in addition to activity information.
The card identifies its holder and is personal: it cannot be transferred to another driver.
The driver card is valid for five years from issue and must be renewed when it expires.
Cards interact with the tachograph: they identify the user and enable different functions, such as recording activities or viewing data.
The tachograph card identifies the driver and records their activities; the CQC certifies professional qualification. Their functions differ.
The driver card is personal: it identifies the driver and stays with them when they change vehicle or employer.
The driver card is valid for five years, not ten.

Before setting off, insert the card while the vehicle is stationary and follow the tachograph’s instructions. For example, the ADR version of the VDO DTCO 4.1x requires the ignition to be on for this function.
The driver at the wheel inserts their card in slot 1. After reading it, the tachograph displays the name associated with the card.

At the end of a shift, if rest begins, select rest before ejecting the card. If instead you are doing other work or are available, record the actual activity; enter subsequent periods away from the vehicle manually when required.
The card records driving and must be inserted before driving begins; there is no required sequence relative to inserting the ignition key.
Insert the card before starting to drive, not while moving, so activities can be recorded from the start.
OUT identifies use outside scope; rest describes a driver activity. Driving outside scope does not become rest.
In Italy, the request to block and/or replace the card goes to the Chamber of Commerce within seven days of discovering the event.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but the rule requires a printout of vehicle details at the start of the journey, with name, card or licence number, signature and relevant periods; an activity printout is also needed at the end. A technical-data printout alone has not been shown to be equivalent.
At the end of the journey, print the time records, add any unrecorded periods, and identify and sign for the driver.
The quiz marks this TRUE, but periods already captured on the analogue chart need not be duplicated on the digital card. Keep the chart, insert the card and record any genuinely missing periods.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but changing vehicles does not always require a printout. Complete and use the analogue chart, and retain the card and required records. A printout can help, but is not automatically required solely because of the change.
The deadline is not thirty days: the request must be submitted within seven days of discovering the event.
There is no ordinary 45-day permission: the limit is 15 days, except for the time needed to return to base, with proof that the card cannot be used.
The driver must request a replacement and document activities using the required printouts; theft or loss must also be reported to the police.
Theft or loss is reported to the police, not the labour office; damage follows the replacement procedure.
Fifteen days is not the permitted delay for repair: it must be done as soon as possible and, if the vehicle cannot return within one week, en route.
The unit’s memory supports different printouts: daily activities, events and faults, overspeeding and technical data serve different checks.
The overspeed printout documents recorded events, including date, time and maximum speed. It concerns the tachograph’s overspeed threshold, not every road speed limit.
The printout shows overspeed events retained under selective criteria, not a complete record of the last ten years.
The card has limited capacity: older data can be overwritten, so a 365-day activity history is not guaranteed.
A fallen load can obstruct traffic: the driver must remove it and clear the way as far as possible.
If the vehicle cannot be moved, the obstruction remains a danger to approaching traffic and must be signalled to other road users.

Outside built-up areas the triangle warns of a stopped vehicle in the specified conditions, for example when it cannot be seen from a sufficient distance. The obstruction must in any case be signalled.
In built-up areas placing the triangle is not always mandatory. The obstruction must still be signalled by suitable means according to the circumstances.
Dangerous substances must not be channelled into a sewer: when safe and appropriate, prevent their entry and contain the spill instead.
Clear the obstruction as promptly as possible and warn other road users; also inform the road authority or the police.
Even when only property is damaged, a person involved in an accident connected with their conduct must stop and give the injured parties their details and other useful information.
Stopping and providing useful information helps the injured parties reconstruct what happened and pursue their claims, even when no one is injured.
The form collects the details of both vehicles and the circumstances in one document, making it easier to report the accident to the insurer.

Warn approaching traffic promptly without exposing yourself to danger, and notify the police or road authority. Use the warning triangle when required or other suitable means if it is unavailable: remaining to signal by hand is not always necessary.
A person involved in an accident connected with their conduct must stop and provide the assistance injured people need.
If the accident is connected with the driver’s conduct and people are injured, failure to assist is punishable by imprisonment; fleeing an accident involving personal injury is also punishable.
Fleeing an accident connected with one’s conduct can lead to arrest when people are injured; the rules differ when only property is damaged.
For negligent personal injury, a driver who stops, gives the necessary assistance and immediately makes themselves available to the judicial police is not subject to arrest in the act.
If the carriageway is obstructed, warn others and inform the road authority or a police body. If you cannot clear the road, their intervention can help manage the obstruction.
If people are injured, stop and provide assistance; call medical emergency services. It is also prudent to notify the police so they can respond and help manage the incident.
It is not optional: even with property damage alone, a person involved in an accident connected with their conduct must stop and give their details to the injured parties.
This is more than advice: stopping and providing personal details are obligations even when an accident connected with one’s conduct causes only property damage.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but a CAI accident form can also be used when more than two vehicles are involved: IVASS instructions provide for two forms for three vehicles. Using the form is distinct from the conditions for direct compensation.
The place and circumstances are not enough: the form also asks for other information, including the date and identification of the vehicles and insurers.
The other driver's details alone are not enough: the form also records the vehicles, policyholders, insurers and circumstances of the accident.
There is no permission to leave the danger in place for an hour: make traffic safe and, where possible, avoid obstructing it.
Stopping is not enough: anyone involved in an accident connected to their conduct must also provide necessary assistance to anyone injured.
When there is only property damage, failure to stop carries an administrative penalty; imprisonment for failing to stop applies to an accident involving injury.
Do not wait until more than three people are injured: even one injured person may require emergency assistance and intervention by the authorities.

Failure to produce the insurance policy does not by itself require a call to the authorities: vehicle details can be recorded and coverage checked. Police assistance can be requested if problems arise.
Hazard lights warn other road users of the broken-down vehicle and the danger in the tunnel.
If the vehicle can still be moved, reaching an emergency lay-by takes it away from the lane used by other traffic.
Where possible, the emergency lane allows the vehicle to stop outside the traffic lanes.
A stopped vehicle is a hazard in a tunnel: quickly request assistance via 112 or an SOS phone.
Hazard lights are necessary, but stopping immediately in a traffic lane is not the right choice if a safer place can be reached.
Do not rely on nearby drivers: signal the breakdown and request assistance through 112 or an SOS phone.
Towing by a passing motorist is not allowed on a motorway: request an authorized recovery service.
Do not simply wait for your own mechanic: on a motorway, signal the breakdown and request authorized assistance.
After an accident in a tunnel, switch off the engine and leave the key in the ignition so emergency services can move the vehicle if necessary.
After calling the emergency services, give injured people first aid within your abilities and without exposing yourself to danger: it can help preserve life until professionals arrive.

Chocks prevent the vehicle from moving; they do not signal the accident. Securing the vehicle, for example by applying the brake, and calling emergency services take priority; getting out into traffic solely to place chocks is not an automatic response.
Do not make a U-turn in a tunnel: stop the vehicle safely and alert the emergency services.
The driver must promptly clear the road as far as possible by moving the vehicle: approaching vehicles may collide with an obstruction in the carriageway.

Push the vehicle off the carriageway; if that is impossible, place it at the right edge, parallel to the road. This frees as much space as possible for approaching traffic and reduces the risk of a collision.
Whatever its cause, an obstruction can endanger approaching traffic: the driver must remove it and promptly clear the road as far as possible.
Light traffic does not remove the obligation: clear the road as far as possible and move the vehicle off the carriageway or to its right edge.
Do not leave the load on the road to reconstruct the event: remove the obstruction as far as possible and signal the danger.
The rule requires clearing the road as far as possible, not that the driver can quickly repair every heavy-vehicle breakdown.
Outside built-up areas at night, if the rear position or hazard lights are missing or insufficient, the triangle warns approaching drivers of the vehicle stopped on the carriageway.
Outside built-up areas at night, the triangle gives advance warning of a fallen load that cannot be removed, alerting approaching drivers to the obstacle on the carriageway.
Outside built-up areas, even in daylight, if a stopped vehicle cannot be seen clearly from 100 meters, the triangle warns approaching drivers in advance.
Vehicles classified as autoveicoli under Italian law, such as cars, buses and trucks, must carry a warning triangle for use when stopped in the prescribed situations.
Place the triangle at least 50 metres behind the vehicle or obstacle, except where an intersection is closer; it must also be visible from 100 metres.
The triangle must be fully visible to approaching drivers from at least 100 metres; this sighting distance is distinct from its distance behind the obstacle.
It is not optional: outside built-up areas at night, a vehicle stopped on the carriageway must be signalled when its rear lights are missing or ineffective.

150 meters is not the prescribed threshold. Outside built-up areas, the regulation specifies 100 meters for visibility in daylight: not seeing the vehicle at 150 meters does not necessarily mean it cannot be seen at 100. At night, advance warning is required if the rear position or hazard lights are missing or insufficient; the Road Code also requires advance warning at night if the vehicle cannot be seen from a sufficient distance.
It is not optional: outside built-up areas a fallen load not clearly visible from 100 metres must be signalled even by day, even if it occupies only one lane.
The specific triangle rule for a stopped vehicle with missing or ineffective lights applies to carriageways outside built-up areas; it does not automatically apply inside them.
Place the triangle on the road behind the obstacle, not on top of the load, to warn approaching vehicles in time.
The triangle must be fully visible to approaching vehicles from at least 100 metres; 50 metres is the ordinary minimum distance behind the obstacle.
Place the triangle in the same lane occupied by the vehicle or obstacle, to warn of the occupied part of the carriageway.
Place the triangle on the carriageway at least one metre from its outer edge, in the lane occupied by the vehicle or obstacle.
Place the triangle in the lane occupied by the vehicle or load, not necessarily in the lane immediately to its left.
The one metre is measured from the outer edge of the carriageway, not from the line separating directions of traffic.
In the prescribed cases, the vest or reflective braces are also required on emergency lanes and in lay-bys: they help approaching drivers see the person placing the warning.

A nighttime breakdown in a built-up area alone does not trigger the obligation to wear a reflective vest or braces. The rule links that obligation to the circumstances requiring advance warning with a triangle outside built-up areas.
The right main mirror gives the driver an indirect view of the road behind on the right side.
The wide-angle mirror expands the visible area beside and behind the vehicle beyond the main mirror’s field.
The passenger-side close-proximity mirror shows the area close to the vehicle, low down beside the door.
The front mirror shows the road immediately in front of the cab, which may be hidden from the driver’s direct view.
The left main mirror gives the driver an indirect view of the road behind on the left side.
The right main mirror covers the rear on the right; the left main mirror is used for the rear on the left.
The wide-angle mirror broadens the view of the road beside and behind the vehicle; it is not for viewing the roof.

The quiz marks this FALSE. For some heavy-vehicle categories, a Class V close-proximity mirror is required on the passenger side; one on the driver side may be optional. The configuration depends on the vehicle.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but some approved camera-monitor systems can replace mirrors under applicable requirements. An arbitrary camera is not enough: approval and required fields of vision matter.
Exterior mirrors must remain in a usable position to observe traffic behind and beside the vehicle on a motorway too; folding them would remove that field of view.
Pillars are opaque parts of the body and can hide objects or road users, creating blind spots.
A high driving position can hide an area close to the front and sides of the cab from direct view.
A poorly positioned load can block the view: it must be arranged so that it does not reduce the driver’s visibility.
Without a rear window there is one fewer opening for a direct view to the rear; exterior mirrors help monitor the area behind.
A transparent rear window normally provides a view behind; its absence, rather than its mere presence, removes that possibility.
The quiz marks this FALSE. Mirrors expand indirect vision, but large mirrors can also obstruct part of the direct view; both effects matter.
The quiz marks this FALSE. Wipers clear the windscreen and improve visibility, but a blade stopped in an abnormal position can obstruct it; check they work correctly.
The mere presence of a fire extinguisher does not itself restrict the view; its position matters and it must not obstruct sight.
Choosing toughened glass alone does not make a windscreen opaque: safety glazing must meet optical requirements, including light transmission.
Papers on the dashboard can reflect in the windshield and obscure the view of the road. Keeping the dashboard clear reduces these reflections.
A worn blade can leave water and streaks in the field of view. Replace it when it no longer clears the glass properly.
In darkness, interior light makes the road ahead harder to see. Keeping it off helps night vision.
Condensation on the glass obscures the view outside. Defogging the windshield and side windows before setting off keeps the field of view clear.
Seat height determines the position of the eyes relative to the windows. Adjust it to see the road well while retaining control of the controls.
Mirrors and cameras show the driver areas around the vehicle that cannot be seen directly through the windows.
These aids expand the view, but do not guarantee visibility of every area around the vehicle. A pedestrian or vehicle can remain in a blind spot.
Correctly adjusted mirrors show the sides better and help drivers spot pedestrians and cyclists while maneuvering, reducing the risk of hitting them.
In a left-hand-drive vehicle, the right side is far from the driver and can hide nearby road users, especially when turning. Check it carefully in the mirrors.
Turning on an interior light does not always improve visibility: in darkness it can make the road ahead harder to see.
Wiper blades are replaced according to how well they clear the glass, not whenever the diesel filter is changed. These are separate maintenance tasks.
Completely covering the window eliminates the side view. A sun visor can help with sunlight while keeping the view clear.
Grease is not a windshield cleaner: it leaves a film that can reduce clarity. Clean the inside of the glass too, without leaving residue.
Mirrors and cameras reduce unseen areas, but do not guarantee complete coverage of every angle around the vehicle.
Check and adjust the mirrors from the driving position before setting off so the necessary view is available immediately. There is no need to wait for the vehicle to settle.
Adjustment aims to provide the correct field of view from the driving position. Wind is not the criterion for aiming the mirrors.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not explain why. Adjust mirrors from your normal driving position to see the required fields clearly, wearing glasses if needed: wearing them alone does not determine one universal mirror setting.
The tachograph card records the driver’s activities; it does not ensure automatic mirror adjustment. Check the mirror view before the journey.
Interior mirrors allow the driver to observe passengers and the door area from the cab, including during boarding and alighting.
Interior mirrors help check people on board and near the doors; exterior mirrors show people nearby outside. Checking before operating the doors helps prevent impacts or trapping.
Before moving off, the driver also checks the interior mirrors to make sure passengers have finished boarding or alighting and are safe.
A poorly aimed interior mirror can hide the door area. The driver could then close the door or move off without seeing someone still boarding or alighting.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but mirror coverage depends on the bus: an interior door mirror can also show the area immediately outside. Check people and doors using the available devices, without assuming every mirror covers the whole stop.
Interior mirrors help the driver observe the passenger compartment; exterior mirrors show other areas. The interior mirrors must also be adjusted correctly.
Some buses have interior mirrors for observing passengers, so it is not true that buses never have interior mirrors.
A trailer changes the view to the sides and rear: adjust the exterior mirrors to monitor the combination and surrounding traffic.
Before returning to the lane, make sure the rear of the trailer has also cleared the overtaken vehicle, checking the right mirrors and blind spots.
When turning, the trailer follows a tighter path than the towing vehicle. Watching it in the mirrors helps prevent it mounting the sidewalk.
When turning, the trailer follows a tighter path than the towing vehicle and can hit someone on the right. Check the mirrors and account for blind spots.
When turning, the semitrailer follows a tighter path than the tractor. Watching it in the mirrors helps prevent it mounting the sidewalk.
When turning, the semitrailer follows a tighter path than the tractor and can hit someone on the right. Check the mirrors and account for blind spots.
During the turn, the angle between the towing vehicle and trailer changes and can hide the right side of the combination from the mirrors. Allow for this blind spot.
Before returning to the lane, make sure the rear of the semitrailer has also cleared the overtaken vehicle, checking the right mirrors and blind spots.
The mirrors let the driver in the towing vehicle see the sides and rear; mirrors facing the towing vehicle are not required on the trailer.

Exceeding 15.50 metres does not in itself require a camera showing the rear of the trailer. Mirrors are used when reversing with a trailer; detection requirements depend on the rules applicable to the vehicle.
During the turn, the angle between the towing vehicle and trailer changes and mirrors can leave areas out of view. They do not always show the entire right-hand end.
Not every combination must have a special enlarged mirror approved for towing. The required devices and field of view depend on the vehicle.
Coupling a trailer does not automatically require mirrors to be replaced. Check that the available mirrors provide an adequate view and are correctly adjusted.
There is no prescribed “towing” position for every mirror. After coupling, check and adjust the view for the combination.
A trailer can be wider than the towing vehicle and restrict the view of the road behind. Check the view with the combination coupled.
The overall centre of gravity depends on the mass and position of the load: changing its type or placement can change the weight distribution.
A high centre of gravity increases rollover risk; too much weight forward or rearward can unbalance axle loads and impair handling.
Keeping the load’s centre of gravity low lowers the overall centre of gravity and reduces the tendency to roll over, all else being equal.
If the shoulder gives way under the wheels, the vehicle can tilt and overturn, especially near the road edge.
Concentrating weight on one side unbalances the vehicle. Distribute the load evenly and close to the centre line.
The side opposite the driver is not where weight should be concentrated: balanced distribution across both sides helps stability.
A higher center of gravity makes a vehicle more prone to rollover, other conditions being equal.
A crosswind can push or destabilize a vehicle even on a straight road, not just on a bend.
On a bend, the liquid collects toward the outside and its push can carry the vehicle off the road.
When braking, inertia carries the liquid toward the front wall, where it can push the vehicle forward.
Baffles reduce liquid movement during maneuvers; their effectiveness also depends on their arrangement, and they do not eliminate all sloshing.
At an intermediate fill level there is both a substantial mass of liquid and room for it to slosh; around half capacity this can make the tank very unstable.
During acceleration, liquid moves toward the rear of the tank, transferring more load to the rear wheels.
Going downhill, liquid tends to collect toward the front of the tilted tank and can push the vehicle forward.
Going uphill, liquid tends to collect toward the rear of the tilted tank, increasing the load on the rear wheels.
On a bend, liquid moves outward, not inward; its lateral push can destabilize the vehicle.
When braking, inertia moves the liquid toward the front wall, not the rear wall.
Baffles mainly limit liquid sloshing; their primary purpose is not to reinforce the structure.
The openings are not solely for cleaning: they also let liquid pass through the baffles, which limit its movement.
An empty tank has no liquid mass to slosh; a partially filled tank may be more prone to rollover because the load moves.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Liquid in a partly filled tank can surge and affect stability; powders can also be hazardous. The comparison depends on the material, fill level, tank, controls and manoeuvre, so there is no universal ranking.
Going uphill, liquid tends to collect toward the rear of the tilted tank, not the front.
The driver must check that the load is properly positioned and secured before setting off.
Payload is the permitted mass of cargo; exceeding it overloads the vehicle beyond its capacity.
The load can shift during the journey, so it must also be checked before unloading, regardless of whether delivery is on private property.

Payload is the permitted mass of the load; there is no 10% allowance based on the water content of the goods. Any weighing reductions apply to the measured mass, not an increase in payload for perishables.
A rear projection of up to three tenths of the vehicle length is allowed only for indivisible items, subject also to overall dimension limits.
A rear projection must be marked with an approved white-and-red striped panel at the end of the load; if it covers the entire rear width, two panels are required at the outer ends.
If the projection spans the entire rear width, two white-and-red panels are needed, one at each end, to indicate its full width.
The general rule prohibits a load from projecting beyond the front of the vehicle; the allowance for indivisible items concerns the rear.

Side projection is measured from the front and rear position lights: it may not exceed 30 cm on each side and must stay within the overall width limit. Hard-to-see horizontal loads such as bars may not project sideways.
One metre is not the general limit for trailers and semi-trailers: indivisible items may project at the rear up to three tenths of vehicle length, within the overall dimension limits.
Three tenths applies to rear projection of indivisible items. At the front, the load generally may not project beyond the vehicle.
Three tenths applies to rear projection, not side projection. The ordinary side limit is 30 cm from the position lights, with further restrictions for hard-to-see loads.
The figure is a yellow-and-red rectangle; rear projection instead requires a retroreflective quadrangular panel with white and red stripes.
The white-and-red panel shown marks a rear longitudinal projection, not two points on the left side. Side projection still requires the prescribed precautions and limits.
Before lifting, the outriggers must bear properly on the ground to support the vehicle and reduce the risk of overturning.
Alternating sides keeps the weight more evenly distributed during unloading and reduces vehicle imbalance.
Raise the tipper body carefully, checking that the material flows and the vehicle remains stable. A person can guide from a safe position, never behind the vehicle during tipping.
The ratchet tensions the strap to restrain the load; the strap and anchor points must be suitable for the load.
Gloves protect the hands during loading and unloading; a helmet and eye protection are used when the risks of the particular operation require them.
Before disconnecting the hoses, wear protection suited to the job: for example, gloves protect the hands and high-visibility clothing makes the worker visible around vehicles.
Properly closing the manhole covers helps prevent liquid escaping during the journey.
The crane must be stowed and secured for transport to prevent uncontrolled movement while driving.
Empty space lets inadequately restrained pallets move during braking or acceleration; a partial load must also be secured.

If material sticks or falls unevenly, the raised body can destabilize and overturn the vehicle. Do not rely on rapid, uninterrupted lifting: lower the body and free the material before raising it again.
Lowering outriggers only on the side where the load is placed is insufficient: stabilise the vehicle according to the crane instructions before lifting.
Unloading an entire row concentrates the weight on the other side and can unbalance the vehicle. Alternating sides keeps the load more even.
Suitable gloves protect against handling risks in summer too: their selection depends on the risks of the work, not the season.

The quiz marks this FALSE: safe log handling depends on planning, suitable equipment, competent operators and an exclusion zone; a signaller may be needed. Length over 7 m alone does not establish a general requirement for a forest officer.
A crane for handling goods does not by itself prohibit a motor vehicle from using a motorway. A vehicle classified as a work machine is different and is subject to the exclusions for that category.
Doors provide ordinary access; emergency exits offer additional escape routes when needed.
On-board extinguishers allow a small fire to be tackled early; they must be suitable for their intended use and kept in working order.

The extinguisher’s periodic inspection is every six months. The quiz calls it “revision”, but inspection is not necessarily the same as a technical overhaul and replacement of the extinguishing agent.

The quiz refers to the equipment specified by the 1977 decree: up to 30 seats, one 5-litre foam extinguisher or one 2 kg CO₂ extinguisher. A later circular also recognises an approved water-based extinguisher of at least 6 litres as equivalent.

The quiz marks this TRUE: a pair of chocks helps prevent a parked heavy vehicle from rolling accidentally, particularly on a steep slope. ASAPS educational guidance describes two chocks for vehicles and trailers over 3.5 tonnes.
The quiz marks this VERO. Wheelchair safety depends on the approved configuration: some use restraints, while eligible rear-facing positions use a suitable support.
One extinguisher must be placed near the driver’s seat so it is within the driver’s reach.

The quiz marks this FALSE: the guidance describes one pair of chocks for heavy vehicles, not a general requirement for two pairs. Chocks resist accidental movement; this does not prohibit carrying extras.
The quiz marks this FALSO. Wheelchair safety depends on the approved configuration: some use restraints, while eligible rear-facing positions use a suitable support.
The requirement is for at least one extinguisher near the driver; it does not require all extinguishers to be placed there.

The quiz marks this FALSE: more than 17 passengers does not by itself determine that two first-aid kits are required. For example, one bus specification with at least 18 seats calls for one kit; check the equipment required for the vehicle.
Twelve months is too long for the periodic inspection: the quiz requires a check every six months. This check is distinct from the extinguisher’s technical overhaul.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but the alternative is ambiguous: under the historical reference for up to 30 seats, 2 litres of foam is below the 5-litre minimum; an appropriate approved 5 kg CO₂ extinguisher can instead meet the 2 kg minimum. Check the requirements applicable to the vehicle.
On M2 and M3 buses, seated occupants over three use the available safety systems; statutory exemptions still apply.
The driver of an interregional bus also uses the available safety system when seated while the vehicle is moving, subject to legal exemptions.
A truck under 3.5 tonnes also belongs to category N: the driver uses the available belt, subject to exemptions.
Seated passengers on an interregional bus normally use the available safety systems; interregional service is not a general exemption.
Not all M3 buses are excluded: for example, type-approval rules provide for belts on class III or B M3 buses. Fitted belts must normally be used, subject to exemptions.
The law also provides exemptions for particular personal conditions: for example, a certified specific contraindication can exempt a person from using a belt.
Reminding passengers of the duty encourages use of the available systems. On M2 and M3 buses, information is also provided through signs or pictograms on seats.
The belt must work properly: periodically checking the webbing, buckle and retractor helps identify defects.
The driver of an interregional bus also uses the available safety system when seated while the vehicle is moving, subject to legal exemptions.
Seated passengers on an interregional bus normally use the available safety systems; interregional service is not a general exemption.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Passengers must be informed when seat belts are required, including by appropriate signs; the driver may also remind them, but this does not establish a universal duty to give each person a verbal reminder.
Belts are not exempt from type approval because they are fitted to a bus: the devices are subject to approval requirements.
Buckling up is not enough if the belt is prevented from working: the law also penalises altering or obstructing its normal operation.
During sudden braking the body continues moving forward: without a belt the driver may strike the interior, including the windshield.
The exemption does not automatically apply to every pregnancy: a certificate from the treating gynaecologist must attest to particular risks caused by using the belt.
The exemption applies to conditions or physical impairments that specifically contraindicate belt use and are covered by the required certificate; a diagnosis alone is not enough.
Airbags supplement the protection of a seat belt and do not exempt occupants from wearing it: where a belt is required, it must be worn even with airbags.
The obligation does not begin at 30 km/h: the belt must also be worn at lower speeds, subject to the prescribed exemptions.
Being over 65 does not automatically grant an exemption: the obligation applies unless a specific exception is met.
The daily duration of driving is not a prescribed exemption: even someone driving over seven hours must wear a belt when required.

Two wheel chocks help prevent a parked vehicle from rolling; one bus specification calls for two. The quiz marks this VERO, but that specification does not establish a universal requirement for every bus: check the equipment prescribed for the vehicle.

The quiz marks this VERO: operational guidance calls for two chocks for trailers over 3.5 tonnes to prevent accidental movement. The rule on use on steep gradients does not specify a number; the guidance alone does not establish a general carriage requirement.
Extinguishers must be secured in suitable locations so they cannot move during travel; at least one must be near the driver.
Extinguishers must be approved and suitable for use in an enclosed space; current portable extinguishers must be type-approved under the applicable rules.
The extinguisher is periodically checked by a trained person at least every six months to verify that it works properly.
The check is recorded on the extinguisher’s maintenance tag, with the date and the maintainer’s identity, so it is clear when and by whom it was performed.

A first-aid kit makes supplies available for initial care. The quiz marks this VERO: the 1977 decree provides spaces for one or more kits, but that text does not specify their quantity or contents based on the authorization. Check the requirements applicable to the vehicle.
Emergency exits must be identifiable: markings help passengers recognize them in an emergency.
Doors, windows and escape hatches can serve as emergency exits when designed and marked for that purpose. A breakable safety window also requires an accessible breaking device.
The central control can also activate the engine stop: for example, this function is specified for AMTS Catania’s natural-gas buses.
Fire extinguishers and emergency exits are separate safety provisions: extinguishers are not required only when exits are absent.
A periodic vehicle inspection does not automatically require replacement of the extinguisher; it must be maintained and checked according to its own schedule.
Inspection must be performed and recorded by competent personnel; being the driver alone does not qualify someone to certify it. A driver may do so if also appropriately competent.
The extinguisher check is recorded on its maintenance tag, not on the vehicle registration document.
Foam is not the only option: the decree also provides for carbon dioxide extinguishers and allows suitable equivalents.
The six-monthly check verifies that the extinguisher works; emptying and recharging are separate operations, not required at every check.
The emergency button in this question stops the engine; doors use separate controls and do not all open immediately.
The extinguisher must remain in its designated location and be easy to retrieve in an emergency; winter does not justify storing it in the luggage compartment.
The six-monthly periodic check is more frequent than a twelve-month check; waiting a year does not meet that interval.
The result must be recorded on the tag attached to the extinguisher so it can be checked on board; keeping a record only at the company does not replace that entry.
Clean, intact mirrors adjusted for the driver allow the available side and rear areas to be checked before setting off.
Mirrors extend the field of view, but blind spots can remain where a road user is not visible.
The driver sees some areas directly through the windows; mirrors show other side and rear areas indirectly.
Correct adjustment improves visibility, but does not necessarily eliminate every blind spot around the vehicle.
Mirrors on the two sides show different areas; working mirrors on one side do not restore the view lost on the other.

The quiz marks this FALSE: simply fitting any cameras in place of mirrors is not enough. On eligible vehicles, approved camera-monitor systems may replace specified mirrors subject to the applicable fields of view and conditions; cameras are not universally prohibited.
The manufacturer’s schedule specifies preventive maintenance and its intervals; following it helps keep the vehicle in working order.
Clean glass and mirrors keep both direct and reflected views clear, so they should be checked before departure.
Check engine oil, coolant and washer fluid before setting off: they lubricate the engine, cool it and help keep the windscreen clean, respectively.
Checking brake fluid and wiper blades helps identify braking or visibility problems. For batteries with accessible electrolyte, check its level according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
A dirty windscreen can interfere with the wipers; cleaning the glass and rubber helps them work properly.
The glass must provide visibility from the start: it may become dirty during the journey, but that does not remove the need to check it beforehand.

Do not rule out checking for brake leaks because the vehicle belongs to someone else: finding a leak before departure helps avoid using a defective system. The question concerns a driver’s check, distinct from maintenance.
Clean, intact mirrors adjusted for the driver provide the intended field of view and help identify other road users.
The mirror on the other side cannot restore the view lost through a dirty or damaged mirror; both must be kept in working order.
A general check before a journey can reveal defects that compromise safety, for example in lights, tyres or brakes.
After starting, check the fault warning lights and instruments: a fault light that stays on may indicate a problem to investigate before departure.
Checking levels helps identify insufficient lubrication, coolant or brake fluid; the last applies to systems that use it.
Effective wiper blades and sufficient washer fluid allow the windscreen to be cleaned and visibility maintained.
Headlights help the driver see and be seen; indicators communicate turns. Checking them before departure helps reveal faults.
Reflectors must be intact and clean to reflect other vehicles’ lights and make the vehicle visible.
Cuts, incorrect pressure or insufficient tread can compromise safety. Check all tyres against the requirements applicable to the vehicle.
Required equipment depends on the vehicle and its use. Checking that it is present and intact makes it available when needed.
Where digital tachograph rules apply, the driver and operator must ensure correct operation and proper use of the driver card.
A charged spare battery is not generally required on board; instead, check that the installed battery is secure and in good condition.
Night travel does not generally require two 25-litre fuel cans. Before departure, check the vehicle and the fuel needed for the journey.
Calling the company for permission is not a general mandatory check before every journey; the driver must ensure the vehicle is roadworthy.
There is no general requirement to carry a spare 10-litre can of water; checking the vehicle’s coolant level is useful.
There is no general requirement to carry 10 litres of spare oil; checking the engine oil level before a journey is useful.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Before cold weather, check the level and freeze protection of the specified coolant mixture; do not assume the reserve quantity in the question applies to every journey. Follow any vehicle or fleet instructions as well.
Roadworthiness checks are needed before a journey even for a new vehicle; they do not depend on two years having passed since registration.
The registration certificate identifies the vehicle and its characteristics; consult the manufacturer’s manual for checks and maintenance.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Check pressure periodically according to the manufacturer, using the cold-tyre reference; after driving, follow the instructions for hot tyres. The fleet or journey conditions may call for additional checks.
Lights should also be checked before a daytime journey: they are safety devices and may be needed on the way.
Tyres heat up during travel and their pressure rises. Measuring them cold allows comparison with the specified pressure.
Belts can deteriorate: periodically checking their condition and tension helps detect problems before a belt breaks.
Terminals need to be secure: a faulty connection can impair electrical contact. Check them safely.

On vehicles with hydraulic power steering, check the fluid level periodically as directed by the manufacturer: a low level may indicate a leak, and operating with too little fluid can damage the system.
Checking washer fluid allows the washers to clean the windows when needed and maintain visibility.
The filter traps impurities in the intake air. Keeping it clean helps maintain the correct air-fuel mixture needed for combustion.
Reporting a serious defect promptly lets the company arrange repairs and avoid using an unsafe vehicle.
The periodic roadworthiness inspection must be current for the vehicle category. It does not replace pre-journey checks.
When a vehicle is subject to tachograph requirements, the device also needs periodic checks by an authorised workshop, separate from the vehicle inspection.
Tread over three millimetres does not permit every combination: for type approval of category M, N and O vehicles, tyres normally fitted to the same axle are of the same type.
Setting valve timing is a technical job for competent personnel; the driver’s role includes checks and reporting faults.
Identifying and reporting faults helps, but the driver need not personally diagnose every fault to reduce fuel use; driving and maintenance matter too.
After a successful inspection, the result is recorded on a label on the registration certificate; the driver does not have to sign it.
The driver must not dismantle it: the undertaking has an approved workshop or fitter repair the tachograph. Meanwhile the driver records the periods not recorded by it.
Worn pads need competent brake-system service; the driver should report the problem, not necessarily replace them personally.

The quiz marks FALSO: even small damage needs assessment of its position, visibility and glass condition. The 2026 MIT circular permits some repaired chips to pass inspection only if all conditions and certification requirements are met.
Damaged blades should be replaced: they must be able to clear the windscreen and provide visibility even when no rain is forecast.
The specified pressure can vary with the load: choose the value appropriate to the load using the manufacturer’s instructions.

Checks and repairs keep the vehicle fit for service and help prevent faults that could compromise transport safety and continuity.

Smooth driving, avoiding unnecessary harsh acceleration and braking, reduces stress and wear on mechanical components.
Smooth driving reduces wear on parts such as brakes and tyres, limiting the need to replace them.
Maintenance can limit noise: for example, a damaged silencer can make the exhaust noisy and needs repair.
Maintaining the vehicle according to the manufacturer’s instructions helps reduce harmful emissions caused by inefficient components.

The supply pressure must be checked; in systems with a load-sensing brake valve, the device adjusts braking to the load rather than the driver adjusting pressure each time.

Load placement affects the center of gravity and stability. Keeping the load low and near the center line helps keep the vehicle stable.
Worn shock absorbers do not guarantee fuel savings: they control oscillations less effectively and can impair road holding.
Less damping does not improve comfort: it allows the body to continue oscillating and bouncing.
